item.description: Pathology remains central to clinical diagnosis, yet adoption of digital pathology is constrained by financial, operational, and workflow burdens of fully digital infrastructure. We introduce HistoCAM, a platform for ambient, real-time datafication and digitization of glass-slide microscopy that preserves microscope workflows. A 31-megapixel, high space-bandwidth-time-product camera and custom software application stream and composite the pathologist’s eyepiece view, passively generating multi-resolution images from 2X to 40X while recording magnification use, search paths, and dwell times. These outputs provide immediate workflow uplift through digital annotation, measurement, quality assurance, and real-time integration of configurable AI tools. Simultaneously, HistoCAM links image content with expert interaction data and supports rapid generation of annotated, pre-embedded training data during routine slide review. item.title: 【AI agent】 Filter By:
item.description: Human decision-making is increasingly augmented by artificial intelligence (AI), yet individuals vary in whether they revise their judgments after receiving AI-generated input. We examined how trait mindfulness and creative self-efficacy (CSE), together with communal-agentic personality orientations, relate to decision revision following AI input. Data from 549 UK-based professionals were analysed using binary logistic regression, with revision of the initial budget allocation (change versus no change) as the outcome. The mindfulness × CSE interaction was significant, indicating that the association between mindfulness and decision revision varied by CSE. The pattern was positive at lower CSE and negative at higher CSE, although neither median-split simple slope reached conventional significance. CSE showed no independent main effect. Communal-femininity moderated the association between mindfulness and revision, whereas the hypothesised mindfulness × CSE × communal-femininity interaction was trend-level and is treated as suggestive. item.title: 【Self-driving laboratories】 Filter By:
item.description: Biomaterials underpin diverse clinical and technological applications, including orthopaedic implants, resorbable scaffolds, soft-tissue hydrogels and biosensing interfaces. Their design remains challenging because performance depends on the simultaneous optimization of mechanical, chemical and biological properties across composition, processing conditions and multi-scale structure. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) can be used to accelerate this process by modelling process–structure–property relationships, prioritizing informative experiments and supporting more systematic, data-guided design. These approaches can accelerate biomaterials discovery by enabling rapid property prediction, candidate generation and experiment prioritization across diverse material classes. In this Review, we survey these core methodologies alongside public datasets to illustrate their applications across four major biomaterial classes: metals, polymers, ceramics, and biological materials.
